summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults is legal in Madagascar, but only from age 21. Penal Code Article 331 treats same-sex acts involving a person under 21 as indecent assault, carrying five to ten years' imprisonment, so the age of consent is unequal and a visitor whose partner or counterparty is under 21 faces a serious criminal exposure that a heterosexual visitor does not.

Status on arrival is thin. There is no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, no anti-discrimination law, and no legal gender recognition, so a trans traveller holds no locally recognised identity, no partner status and no named protection under Malagasy law.

The social environment is the dominant practical factor. Homosexuality is not illegal, yet it is widely considered socially unacceptable, and LGBT Malagasy people conceal their lives in order to keep jobs and live in peace, relying on private networks and coded language. A trans visitor is read through that same expectation of concealment, and visible gender non-conformity carries the social cost that local LGBT people manage by hiding.

Official posture is hostile to protection. At Madagascar's fourth universal periodic review in January 2025, the government rejected United Nations recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent. Six Malagasy organisations — Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+ — stated that refusing to act endorses impunity and condones violence.

Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are documented rather than hypothetical: the United States State Department's 2011 human rights report recorded societal discrimination and violence against the LGBT community in Madagascar alongside unlawful killings under the post-coup regime.
tangentialFactors:
Madagascar's decriminalisation sits within a wider continental shift: by July 2020 roughly 22 of 53 African states had moved to decriminalise same-sex conduct, and Madagascar is counted among them, though its over-21 carve-out keeps it out of full legal equality with those jurisdictions.

Assessments of the country's legal framework describe it as limited in progress when compared with other states, with LGBT people facing discrimination and an absence of civic rights despite the removal of criminal penalties.

The 2011 State Department reporting period followed a coup, with unlawful killings recorded and state institutions degraded; that context bears on how much protection any Malagasy authority was capable of extending to LGBT people at the time, and the report's discrimination and violence findings are the most concrete official documentation in the available sources.

Civil society has been the active counterweight. The six organisations that responded to the January 2025 review recommendations form the clearest evidence of organised advocacy, and their public statement frames government refusal as endorsement of violence rather than mere inaction.
localsOnly:
Malagasy LGBT people organise through private networks and coded language, a survival strategy developed because openness costs employment and peace of mind. There is no civic payoff for coming out: marriage and adoption are unavailable to same-sex couples, and the range of civic rights is narrow.

Local organisations working on these issues include Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+, all of which publicly challenged the government's position after the January 2025 universal periodic review.

Resources compiled by Rights in Exile (AsyLex) for Madagascar cover Penal Code Article 331, general societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ people, state-protection capacity, case law and supporting organisations, and are the most concentrated domestic reference point available.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory for this pass contains no material on legal gender recognition or on the existence or absence of an anti-discrimination statute. Those elements are carried forward from the standing record and remain unverified against a source here.

No source in the inventory documents how Article 331 has been enforced: there is no case, charge or conviction cited, and Rights in Exile's reference to case law is not specified. Whether the under-21 provision is used against adults in practice is unresolved.

No source addresses police treatment of trans visitors specifically, entry or visa screening that could disclose gender history, or access to gender-affirming care. The absence of documented police targeting in these materials is not evidence that none occurs.

Dating is inconsistent for one source: the France 24 'Focus' report is labelled August 2024 in the inventory while its URL indicates April 2024. The most recent item overall is dated 17 July 2025, so conditions after that date are not covered.
